title: What GCP training does ICH E6(R3) require, and how often?
description: What ICH E6(R3) good clinical practice requires for trial staff qualification, delegated training, and computerised systems training, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: ICH E6(R3), the International Council for Harmonisation guideline for good clinical practice (GCP), requires everyone involved in a clinical trial to be qualified by education, training, and experience for their tasks. Investigators must train delegated staff in trial activities beyond their usual training, and users of computerised systems must be trained in their use. The guideline sets no fixed refresher interval: training is driven by role, risk, and the trial itself.
keyTakeaways: Principle 5 states that clinical trials "should be designed and conducted by qualified individuals", qualified "by education, training and experience" for their tasks.

The European Medicines Agency (EMA) applies the E6(R3) Principles and Annex 1 from July 23, 2025; Annex 2, on decentralized, pragmatic, and real-world data elements, comes into effect on January 15, 2027.
Annex 1 section 2.3.2 requires trial-related training for delegated persons that corresponds to what they need for activities beyond their usual training and experience.
Section 4.3.2 requires that "those using computerised systems are appropriately trained in their use", and trial-specific training records are listed as essential records in Appendix C.
No passage of the Principles, Annex 1, or Annex 2 reviewed for this page sets a fixed GCP refresher interval such as every two or three years.
jurisdiction: International (ICH guideline; applied by the European Medicines Agency in the EU and issued as final guidance by the US FDA)
regulator: International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH); applied by regulators such as the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
appliesTo: Sponsors of interventional clinical trials of investigational products, including contract research organizations and other service providers acting for them
Investigators, institutions, and investigator site staff to whom trial activities are delegated
Monitors, auditors, data managers, biostatisticians, and others performing trial-related activities
Institutional review boards and independent ethics committees (IRB/IEC), whose members should collectively have the qualifications and experience to review a trial

sections.heading: What is ICH E6(R3) and when does it apply?

blocks.text: ICH E6(R3) is the third revision of the international GCP guideline, reached under Step 4 by the regulatory members of the ICH Assembly on January 6, 2025. It replaces E6(R2) and is structured as overarching Principles, Annex 1 (the detailed expectations for IRB/IEC, investigators, sponsors, and data governance), and Annex 2 (additional considerations for trials using decentralized elements, pragmatic elements, or real-world data).
The guideline itself is not law; each regulator adopts it into its own framework. As at November 2026, verified adoptions include:

Other ICH members, including regulators in Japan and Australia, implement ICH guidelines on their own timelines; check the national regulator before relying on a date.

sections.heading: What do the E6(R3) Principles require for qualification and training?

blocks.text: Principle 5 makes qualification a GCP principle in its own right. Every person doing trial work must be qualified for their specific task through education, training, and experience, not just hold a generic certificate.

blocks.title: ICH E6(R3) Principle 5 and 5.1
blocks.text: "Clinical trials should be designed and conducted by qualified individuals." "Individuals with different expertise and training may be needed across all phases of a clinical trial, such as physicians, nurses, pharmacists, scientists, ethicists, technology experts, trial coordinators, monitors, auditors and biostatisticians. Individuals involved in a trial should be qualified by education, training and experience to perform their respective task(s)."

The Principles also set the frame for how much training is enough: trial processes and risk mitigation "should be proportionate to the importance of the data being collected and the risks to trial participant safety and the reliability of trial results." Training effort should follow the same proportionality, heavier where errors would affect participant safety or critical data.

sections.heading: What does Annex 1 require of investigators, sponsors, and their staff?

blocks.text: Annex 1 turns the principle into role-specific duties. The investigator must be qualified and must make sure delegated staff are qualified and informed; the sponsor must use qualified individuals and check investigator qualifications.

blocks.text: Section 2.3.2 is the key sentence for site training design. It reads: "Trial-related training to persons assisting in the trial should correspond to what is necessary to enable them to fulfil their delegated trial activities that go beyond their usual training and experience." A research nurse taking blood pressure in the usual way may need little trial-specific training for that task, while the same nurse administering a protocol-specific rating scale needs targeted training and a record of it.

sections.heading: What training does E6(R3) require for computerized systems?

blocks.text: E6(R3) requires training for everyone who uses a computerized system in a trial. Section 4.3.2 (Training) states: "The responsible party should ensure that those using computerised systems are appropriately trained in their use."

The sponsor carries an additional duty. Under section 3.16.1(x)(ii), when using computerized systems the sponsor should make sure that "documented procedures and adequate training are in place to ensure the correct development, maintenance and use of computerised systems in clinical trials", proportionate to the importance of the system and the data it processes. In practice this covers electronic data capture, interactive response technology, electronic patient-reported outcome tools, and safety databases, and it reaches site staff, monitors, and data managers.

Annex 2 extends the same logic to new methods. Section 3.2.4 says the methodologies used in a trial "should be considered when determining the need for appropriate training and technical support to be provided to the investigator, investigator site staff and participants". Where trial activities are part of usual clinical practice and require knowledge of trial documents, delegated healthcare professionals "who have been appropriately trained" should perform them.

sections.heading: How often must GCP training be repeated under E6(R3)?

blocks.text: E6(R3) sets no fixed refresher interval. None of the passages on qualification and training in the Principles, Annex 1, or Annex 2 reviewed for this page names a period such as annual, two-yearly, or three-yearly GCP refresher training.

Instead, the guideline ties training to the person's tasks and the trial. A training need arises when someone is delegated a new trial activity, when the protocol or a computerized system changes, when the sponsor introduces a new methodology, and when monitoring or audit finds a gap. Fixed refresher cycles seen in practice usually come from sponsor or institution procedures, not from E6(R3). Organizations that keep one should record the risk rationale, as described in [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

blocks.title: Reading the guideline correctly
blocks.text: E6(R3) asks whether a person is qualified for the task in front of them. A current generic GCP certificate does not by itself show that, and an older certificate does not by itself show the opposite. The evidence that matters is task-specific.

sections.heading: What training records does E6(R3) expect?

blocks.text: Appendix C lists training and qualification evidence as essential records. It includes relevant documents evidencing the qualifications of investigators and sub-investigators (for example curricula vitae), "Trial-specific training records", and documentation of delegation, each marked as records that should generally be in place before the trial starts.

Section C.1 also describes essential records as those that document that sponsor personnel and people performing significant trial activities for the sponsor, and the investigator and delegated individuals, "are qualified by education, training and experience to undertake their activities", particularly where the activities are not part of their normal role. For assembling them, see [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

blocks.text: The underlying method is the same as for any regulated role: define competence first, then assess it. See [competency assessment](/glossary/competency-assessment) and [how to design competency assessments](/guides/how-to-design-competency-assessments).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models E6(R3) provisions, protocol procedures, systems, and trial roles as linked concepts with assessment points. When a protocol amendment or system change occurs, the affected roles and delegated tasks are identified from those links, and the evidence trail shows which version each person was trained and assessed on. See the approach for [healthcare and life sciences](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences).

faqs.q: Does ICH E6(R3) require GCP refresher training every two or three years?
faqs.a: No. The Principles, Annex 1, and Annex 2 passages reviewed for this page set no fixed interval. E6(R3) requires people to be qualified by education, training, and experience for their tasks, so retraining is driven by new delegated activities, protocol and system changes, and identified gaps. Fixed cycles come from sponsor or institutional policy.

faqs.q: Is a generic GCP certificate enough under E6(R3)?
faqs.a: Not on its own. A certificate can evidence general GCP knowledge, but section 2.3.2 requires trial-related training for delegated activities beyond a person's usual training and experience, and Appendix C lists trial-specific training records as essential records. Inspectors look for both.

faqs.q: Do participants need training under E6(R3)?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Annex 2, which takes effect in the EU on January 15, 2027, says the methodologies used should be considered when determining training and technical support for investigators, site staff, and participants, for example where participants use digital health technologies at home.

faqs.q: Who is responsible for computerized system training?
faqs.a: The responsible party for the system. Section 4.3.2 says the responsible party should ensure users are appropriately trained, and section 3.16.1(x)(ii) requires the sponsor to have documented procedures and adequate training in place for the correct development, maintenance, and use of computerized systems.
